extracted.intended_audience: novelists, creative-writing students, and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for novelists on the fundamental aspects of the novel—how to handle story/time, narrative voice, setting/space, and the creation and treatment of characters (birth, death, food, sleep, love).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense of space
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession of a sense of space (as opposed to merely a feeling for place) is a high quality in a novelist: ‘‘Very few have the sense of space, and the possession of it ranks high in Tolstoy’s divine equipment. Space is the lord of War and Peace, not time.’’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use expansive, accumulated descriptions of landscape, bridges, rivers, forests, roads, gardens and fields to produce an effect like music — great chords that do not arise from episodes or characters but from the sum-total of place. Space can exhilarate and prevent a novel from feeling merely depressing even when it shows decay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story as sequence / the novel tells a story
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel fundamentally ‘tells a story’ — a constant ‘‘and then ... and then,’’ i.e. a sequence in chronology, is the novel’s sole contribution in this inquiry: ‘‘the novel tells a story.’’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect chronological sequence as a basic structural element; recognize that attempts to abolish temporal sequence risk destroying intelligibility and valuable narrative order unless replaced by an equally effective substitute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative voice appeals to the ear
rubrics_metrics.description: The story is the repository of a voice that asks to be read out loud and appeals to the ear rather than merely the eye: ‘‘It is the aspect of the novelist’s work which asks to be read out loud... it adds something because of its connection with a voice.’’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate a speaking narrator / tribal storyteller quality where appropriate. Consider how sentences and openings work when recited (even if prose-level melody can be gathered by the eye). Use voice deliberately to transform readers into listeners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story vs author’s personality
rubrics_metrics.description: The story/voice is not the same as the author’s personality and does not convey the author’s personality as strongly as characters, plot, or comments on life: ‘‘It does not give us anything as important as the author’s personality.’’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convey authorial temperament primarily through characters, plot and commentary rather than relying solely on narrative voice; avoid confusing voice with full autobiographical or authorial self-expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of abolishing time (experimentation limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental attempts to abolish time in fiction (e.g., Gertrude Stein’s work) fail because once fiction is completely delivered from time it often cannot express anything intelligibly: ‘‘the novel that would express values only becomes unintelligible and therefore valueless.’’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If experimenting with non-chronological forms, ensure you do not also unintentionally destroy sentence or word order to the point of unreadability; maintain alternative structures that preserve intelligibility and meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: The novel’s primitive/tribal appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: The story aspect of the novel is primitive and appeals to primitive parts of us — the tribal narrator telling events until listeners fall asleep — and this creates strong, sometimes intolerant reader loyalties: ‘‘The story is primitive... That is why we are so unreasonable over the stories we like.’’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge and harness the story’s primal appeal, but be aware it generates strong reactions and intolerance among readers; use the story’s directness deliberately rather than apologetically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters should reveal hidden life (fiction vs history)
rubrics_metrics.description: A novelist’s task is to reveal the hidden inner life of characters — to tell us more about people than history can: ‘‘It is the function of the novelist to reveal the hidden life at its source: to tell us more about Queen Victoria than could be known.’’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use invented interiority and imaginatively constructed motives to create characters distinct from historical memoirs; exploit fiction’s license to expose inner thoughts, emotions and romantic sides that history cannot record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference between novel-people and historical people
rubrics_metrics.description: People in novels can be understood completely by the reader (inner and outer life can be exposed) whereas people in daily life and history remain partly opaque: ‘‘people in a novel can be understood completely by the reader, if the novelist wishes.’’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide how much of a character’s inner life to disclose — full disclosure can make them more definite than real people; use this advantage intentionally to serve the novel’s aims rather than as mere convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create physical, concrete characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should be given physicality and concrete small details (height, weight, breathing, actions) so they feel like living beings rather than abstract types: e.g., Moll Flanders moves us ‘as having height and weight, as breathing and eating.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include sensory, bodily, and habitual details (movements, gestures, appetites) casually and unobtrusively to provide verisimilitude; small, everyday actions often convey character more effectively than heavy psychological exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of birth in fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Birth is rarely fully explored in fiction; babies in novels often appear ‘off’ or posted and are put into cold storage until useful: ‘‘When a baby arrives in a novel it usually has the air of having been posted.’’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you choose to depict birth or early infancy, consider the untapped psychological/literary potential; beware of treating births purely as plot devices—either omit thoughtfully or explore baby psychology purposefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of death in fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Death is congenial to novelists and often used effectively to conclude books; the novelist can work from the known toward the darkness and be both appropriate and imaginative: ‘‘The treatment of death... has a variety about it which suggests that the novelist finds it congenial.’’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build toward deaths through accumulated characterization so the ending feels earned; avoid relying on superficial or sensational 'seance' material about an afterlife — imaginative empathy and attention to the life lived make death powerful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Food as a social device (not physiological)
rubrics_metrics.description: Food in fiction tends to be mainly social — it draws characters together — rather than a fully physiologically or sensuously-realized necessity: ‘‘Food in fiction is mainly social... seldom enjoy it, and never digest it unless specially asked to do so.’’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scenes of eating to reveal relationships, status, ritual and interaction; if you want the sensuality of food, attend to its aesthetic/sensuous aspects rather than treating meals as mere social props.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sleep and dreams are often underused
rubrics_metrics.description: Sleep occupies a large portion of life but fiction treats it perfunctorily; dreams in novels are usually logical or patched mosaics rather than a reconstruction of the dream world: ‘‘No attempt to indicate oblivion or the actual dream world.’’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether and how to represent sleep and dreams: either integrate them meaningfully into the character’s life or intentionally reconstruct dream states to expand the novel’s temporal and psychological range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love’s prominence can be excessive and monotone
rubrics_metrics.description: Love (especially sex) dominates novels disproportionately and can make them monotonous; two reasons are novelist-created sensitivity and convenience for endings (marriage/permanence): ‘‘I am using this celebrated word in its widest... Love bulks in novels, and will probably agree... it has done them harm.’’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overemphasizing constant romantic sensitiveness in characters; ensure love-motivations are credible and varied, and resist using love only as an easy device to conclude or to create illusory permanence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of novelist’s temperament shaping evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A novel is not pure evidence: the novelist’s temperament (the unknown quantity) modifies and sometimes transforms factual evidence: ‘‘A novel is based on evidence + or − X; the unknown quantity being the temperament of the novelist.’’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remain conscious of how your own biases and temperament color characterization, plot and interpretation of facts. Use that shaping deliberately, but don’t mistake subjective shaping for objective record when realism is intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical traits of fictional people (Homo Fictus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fictional people tend to be born 'off', capable of dying on, require little food or sleep, are tirelessly occupied with relationships, and are more knowable than real people because creator and narrator are one: ‘‘Homo Fictus ... is generally born off, ... wants little food or sleep, he is tirelessly occupied with human relationships.’’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to conform to or subvert these tendencies. If you make characters more like real people (needs, hidden lives, ordinary time spent asleep/eating), plan how that affects pacing, plot and reader expectations.
